items.question: Examine the instruments of monetary policy available to the Reserve Bank of India and evaluate the effectiveness of the flexible inflation-targeting framework in achieving price stability.
items.modelAnswer:
## Introduction

Monetary policy is the RBI's principal instrument for managing the money supply and interest rates to secure **price stability while supporting growth**. Since 2016, India has operated a statutory **flexible inflation-targeting (FIT)** framework anchored on a 4% (±2%) CPI target.

## Instruments of monetary policy

- **Quantitative (general) tools** influence overall liquidity:
  - **Repo rate** (introduced under the LAF, 2000) — the policy anchor; the **SDF** (2022) forms the corridor floor and the **MSF/Bank Rate** the ceiling.
  - **CRR** (cash with RBI) and **SLR** (liquid assets with the bank) regulate lendable resources.
  - **OMO** (1992) and the **MSS** (2004) inject or sterilise liquidity.
- **Qualitative tools** — margin requirements, moral suasion and selective credit control direct credit to specific sectors.
- Decisions are taken by the **six-member Monetary Policy Committee**, which meets at least four times a year, giving policy transparency and continuity.

## Effectiveness of the FIT framework

- **Strengths:** anchored inflation expectations, reduced the earlier volatility of double-digit inflation, and enhanced RBI credibility and independence; the ±2% band gives flexibility to support growth during shocks.
- **Limitations:** monetary policy is weak against **supply-side/cost-push inflation** (food, fuel), which dominates Indian CPI; **transmission** to lending rates is slow because of high small-savings rates and bank NPAs; and a single national rate cannot address **regional price differences**.

## AP angle

For an agrarian state like **Andhra Pradesh**, transmission matters most for **crop loans, MSME and aquaculture credit**; effective rate cuts lower the cost of Kisan Credit Card and MSME finance, aiding rural incomes.

## Conclusion

The FIT framework has delivered greater price stability and policy credibility, but its success depends on **supply-side management, faster transmission and fiscal support** — monetary policy alone cannot ensure durable price stability.
keyPoints: FIT framework (2016): statutory 4% ±2% CPI target set by GoI in consultation with RBI.
Quantitative tools: repo/SDF/MSF corridor, CRR, SLR, OMO, MSS; qualitative tools: margin, moral suasion, selective credit control.
Six-member MPC decides rates, adding transparency and continuity.
Strengths: anchored expectations, lower volatility, RBI credibility and independence.
Limits: weak against supply-side inflation, slow transmission, NPAs, no regional differentiation.
AP relevance: transmission shapes crop-loan, MSME and aquaculture credit costs.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Monetary Policy; Reserve Bank of India; RBI (Sep 2026)

items.question: Discuss the challenge of non-performing assets (NPAs) in the Indian banking sector and analyse how banking reforms and financial-inclusion initiatives seek to build a resilient and inclusive banking system.
items.modelAnswer:
## Introduction

A sound banking system is the backbone of economic growth, mobilising savings and channelling credit. Yet **non-performing assets (NPAs)** — loans on which repayment is overdue beyond 90 days — have periodically stressed Indian banks, particularly public-sector banks, constraining fresh lending.

## The NPA challenge

- **Causes:** over-lending during boom years, wilful defaults, project delays, external shocks and weak credit appraisal.
- **Consequences:** erosion of bank capital, reduced credit flow, and a drag on growth and fiscal resources (recapitalisation).

## Reforms to strengthen banks

- **SARFAESI Act, 2002** — recovery of secured loans without court intervention.
- **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016** — time-bound resolution through the NCLT, shifting from 'debtor-in-possession' to 'creditor-in-control'.
- **Prompt Corrective Action (PCA)** — RBI restrictions on weak banks to arrest deterioration.
- **Bank consolidation (2020)** — merging 10 PSBs into 4 for scale and efficiency; recapitalisation and Basel-III capital norms.

## Financial-inclusion initiatives

- **PM Jan Dhan Yojana (2014)** and the **JAM trinity** brought crores into the formal system, enabling Direct Benefit Transfer.
- **Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks**, **priority-sector lending** (40% target), and **UPI/BBPS** deepened access and digital payments.

## AP angle

In **Andhra Pradesh**, Regional Rural Banks (e.g. Andhra Pradesh Grameena Vikas Bank), SHG-bank linkage and Jan Dhan accounts underpin rural credit and DBT for welfare schemes, aiding inclusion in agrarian and coastal districts.

## Conclusion

A resilient banking system needs **timely NPA resolution, strong governance and adequate capital**, paired with **deepening financial inclusion** — together they make banking both stable and broad-based, serving inclusive growth.
keyPoints: NPA = loan overdue beyond 90 days; causes include over-lending, defaults, project delays, weak appraisal.
Resolution toolkit: SARFAESI 2002, IBC 2016 (NCLT), PCA framework, Basel-III capital norms.
2020 mega-merger consolidated 10 PSBs into 4 for scale and efficiency.
Financial inclusion: PMJDY 2014, JAM trinity, SFBs/Payments Banks, 40% PSL, UPI/BBPS.
AP relevance: RRBs, SHG-bank linkage and Jan Dhan accounts anchor rural credit and DBT.
Resilient + inclusive banking requires both NPA resolution and wider access.
